children.description: A list of children the claimant is claiming for.

lives_with_claimant.description: Whether the child lives with the claimant.

in_approved_education.description: Whether the child is in approved education or training (e.g. A-levels, GCSEs, NVQ up to level 3). Only relevant for children aged 16-19.

in_extension_period.description: Whether the child (aged 16 or 17) has left education and registered with a government-sponsored careers service or the armed forces (qualifying for a 20-week extension).

upkeep_per_week.description: The amount in £ per week the claimant contributes towards the child's upkeep (food, clothes, pocket money, etc.). Only relevant if the child does not live with the claimant.

another_claimant_has_priority.description: Whether another person who also lives with the child has priority for claiming Child Benefit.

another_claimant_lives_with_child.description: Whether someone who lives with the child is already claiming Child Benefit for them.

care_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in local authority care.

care_home_24h_per_week.description: Whether the child spends at least 24 hours per week at home while in local authority care.

hospital_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in hospital or residential accommodation.

claimant_spends_on_child.description: Whether the claimant regularly spends money on the child (e.g. food, clothes, books) while the child is in hospital or residential accommodation.

is_fostered.description: Whether the child is fostered by the claimant.

council_pays_for_child.description: Whether the local council pays towards the child's accommodation or maintenance.

works_24_plus_hours.description: Whether the child works 24 or more hours per week in paid employment.

started_apprenticeship_in_england.description: Whether the child has started an apprenticeship in England.

receives_qualifying_benefits.description: Whether the child receives qualifying benefits in their own right, such as Universal Credit or Employment and Support Allowance.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Hello! I'd be happy to help you determine if you're eligible for Child Benefit.

To assess your eligibility, I need to ask you some questions. Let me start with the basics:

**Do you have any children, and if so, how many children are you inquiring about?**

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Hi! Yes, I have one child - my son Alex. He's 16 and lives at home with me. I wanted to check if I can claim Child Benefit for him?

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for providing that information! I can see you have one child, Alex, who is 16 and lives at home with you.

Since Alex is 16, there are specific rules that apply. You can normally still qualify for Child Benefit for a child who is 16 or over, as long as they are under 20 and they stay in approved education or training.

**Is Alex currently in approved education or training?** (For example, is he in sixth form, college, or an approved training program?)

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Well, he's not in sixth form or college at the moment. He finished his GCSEs and decided not to continue with A-levels or anything like that.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for that information. Since Alex has finished his GCSEs and is not continuing with further education or training, let me ask:

**Has Alex registered with a government-sponsored careers service or the armed services?** 

(This is important because you can apply for Child Benefit to continue for 20 weeks if a 16 or 17 year old leaves education or training and registers with either of these.)

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, he hasn't signed up with anything like that - no careers service or armed forces or anything. He's just been at home trying to figure out what he wants to do next.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for clarifying that. Let me ask a few more questions to complete the assessment:

**Has Alex started any paid work? And if so, is he working 24 hours or more per week?**

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, he's not working at the moment. He doesn't have a job.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you. One more important question:

**Is Alex claiming any benefits in his own right, such as Employment and Support Allowance or Universal Credit?**

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, he's not claiming any benefits himself.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for providing all that information. Let me also confirm a few final details to complete my assessment:

**Do you live in the UK, and are you responsible for Alex (meaning you live with him and provide for his needs)?**

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, I live in the UK - we're here in England. And yes, Alex lives with me and I'm responsible for him.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Based on the information you've provided, I'm sorry to inform you that **you are not eligible for Child Benefit for Alex** at this time.

Here's why:

Since Alex is 16 years old, the rules for Child Benefit change. You can normally still qualify for Child Benefit if your child is under 20 **and** they stay in approved education or training. However, Alex:
- Is not currently in approved education or training (such as sixth form, college, or a training program)
- Has not registered with a government-sponsored careers service or the armed services (which would allow Child Benefit to continue for 20 weeks after leaving education)

**What could change this:**

If Alex were to:
- Enroll in approved education or training (like college, sixth form, or an apprenticeship)
- Register with a careers service or the armed forces (which would give you 20 weeks of Child Benefit)

Then you could potentially claim or restart Child Benefit.

If Alex's circumstances change in the future, you may want to check your eligibility again.
